update.draft:
Dramatic Price Shifts in DRAM: A Decade of Volatility

Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron account for more than 90% of global DRAM revenue. This dominance has made the memory market highly susceptible to supply chain disruptions and demand fluctuations. Without these major players controlling such a large share, price swings would be less extreme—making it harder to predict cost trends or plan budgets in industries reliant on high-speed data access.

The Rise of DDR5: A Quadruple Increase

Standard DDR5 memory prices have risen sharply through 2026. Some 32GB kits climbed from roughly $95 to $250 in mid-2025, reaching as high as $550 to $650 today. This surge has made it increasingly difficult for consumers and businesses alike to upgrade hardware without facing significant cost barriers.

The price increase is driven by a shortage fueled primarily by HBM memory demand. As artificial intelligence applications expand across industries—from healthcare diagnostics to autonomous vehicles—demand for high-bandwidth memory continues to outpace supply, pushing DDR5 prices nearly quadruple in less than two years.

DRAM Price Volatility: From Spikes to Slumps

DRAM prices were spiking during periods of high demand and falling when there was low demand and high supply. These cycles have created a volatile pricing environment where businesses must constantly adapt their purchasing strategies. For example, in Q1 2026, memory prices increased by as much as 80% to 90% compared with the previous quarter (Q4 2025), reflecting an urgent need for semiconductor components.

Conversely, when supply outstripped demand—such as during periods of economic downturn or technological stagnation—DRAM prices dropped significantly. This fluctuation has made it challenging to forecast costs and plan long-term investments in IT infrastructure that depends on memory performance.

The Role of Geopolitical Tensions

Geopolitical tensions between the U.S. and China have affected global trade flows since 2018, with trade between rivals decreasing and friend-shoring increasing. These shifts disrupted traditional supply chains used in semiconductor manufacturing, contributing to price instability.

The pandemic further complicated matters by causing profound disruptions to the globalized model of production and distribution. National lockdowns in 2022 slowed or even temporarily stopped the flow of raw materials and finished goods, disrupting memory chip manufacturing worldwide. While some argue that these challenges were not entirely new—suggesting supply chains have always faced risks—it is clear that recent events accelerated existing vulnerabilities.

DRAM Price Trends: A Market in Flux

The global DRAM market is forecast to approach $400 billion by 2027 due to AI and data centre growth accelerating HBM demand. This projection underscores the rapid expansion of memory requirements as industries embrace more complex computing solutions. The compound annual growth rate (CAGR) for the sector has been estimated at 10.2% from 2025 to 2035, indicating a sustained upward trajectory despite short-term volatility.

However, sources disagree on when this trend will stabilize. Some claim RAM prices are expected to normalize in the 2024–2026 period, while others suggest DRAM prices may continue rising into Q2 2026 with potential surges of up to 70%. This uncertainty highlights how closely tied memory pricing is to broader economic and technological shifts.

A History of Manipulation: The Price Fixing Scandal

Samsung, Micron, and Hynix (predecessor of SK Hynix) were involved in a criminal conspiracy to fix DRAM prices between 1998 and 2002. This illegal activity led to significant price increases that lasted well into the early 2010s. The scandal not only damaged reputations but also created long-term distrust among consumers, investors, and regulators regarding market fairness.

The legacy of this manipulation is still felt today in how closely monitored memory pricing remains. With such a large share of global DRAM production controlled by just three companies—Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron—the potential for future price distortions continues to be a concern for industry stakeholders.

Dramatic Price Shifts in DRAM: A Decade of Volatility

Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron account for more than 90% of global DRAM revenue. This dominance has made the memory market highly susceptible to supply chain disruptions and demand fluctuations. Without these major players controlling such a large share, price swings would be less extreme—making it harder to predict cost trends or plan budgets in industries reliant on high-speed data access.

The Rise of DDR5: A Quadruple Increase

Standard DDR5 memory prices have risen sharply through 2026. Some 32GB kits climbed from roughly $95 to $250 in mid-2025, reaching as high as $550 to $650 today. This surge has made it increasingly difficult for consumers and businesses alike to upgrade hardware without facing significant cost barriers.

The price increase is driven by a shortage fueled primarily by HBM memory demand. As artificial intelligence applications expand across industries—from healthcare diagnostics to autonomous vehicles—demand for high-bandwidth memory continues to outpace supply, pushing DDR5 prices nearly quadruple in less than two years.

DRAM Price Volatility: From Spikes to Slumps

DRAM prices were spiking during periods of high demand and falling when there was low demand and high supply. These cycles have created a volatile pricing environment where businesses must constantly adapt their purchasing strategies. For example, in Q1 2026, memory prices increased by as much as 80% to 90% compared with the previous quarter (Q4 2025), reflecting an urgent need for semiconductor components.

Conversely, when supply outstripped demand—such as during periods of economic downturn or technological stagnation—DRAM prices dropped significantly. This fluctuation has made it challenging to forecast costs and plan long-term investments in IT infrastructure that depends on memory performance.

The Role of Geopolitical Tensions

Geopolitical tensions between the U.S. and China have affected global trade flows since 2018, with trade between rivals decreasing and friend-shoring increasing. These shifts disrupted traditional supply chains used in semiconductor manufacturing, contributing to price instability.

The pandemic further complicated matters by causing profound disruptions to the globalized model of production and distribution. National lockdowns in 2022 slowed or even temporarily stopped the flow of raw materials and finished goods, disrupting memory chip manufacturing worldwide. While some argue that these challenges were not entirely new—suggesting supply chains have always faced risks—it is clear that recent events accelerated existing vulnerabilities.

DRAM Price Trends: A Market in Flux

The global DRAM market is forecast to approach $400 billion by 2027 due to AI and data centre growth accelerating HBM demand. This projection underscores the rapid expansion of memory requirements as industries embrace more complex computing solutions. The compound annual growth rate (CAGR) for the sector has been estimated at 10.2% from 2025 to 2035, indicating a sustained upward trajectory despite short-term volatility.

However, sources disagree on when this trend will stabilize. Some claim RAM prices are expected to normalize in the 2024–2026 period, while others suggest DRAM prices may continue rising into Q2 2026 with potential surges of up to 70%. This uncertainty highlights how closely tied memory pricing is to broader economic and technological shifts.

A History of Manipulation: The Price Fixing Scandal

Samsung, Micron, and Hynix (predecessor of SK Hynix) were involved in a criminal conspiracy to fix DRAM prices between 1998 and 2002. This illegal activity led to significant price increases that lasted well into the early 2010s. The scandal not only damaged reputations but also created long-term distrust among consumers, investors, and regulators regarding market fairness.

The legacy of this manipulation is still felt today in how closely monitored memory pricing remains. With such a large share of global DRAM production controlled by just three companies—Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron—the potential for future price distortions continues to be a concern for industry stakeholders.
